Note: They are not after your stops. The market is just not in a rush in times like this to rally. Momentum is missing. When the markets are in a rush to position and FOMO is the driving force, then we get to see Type 1 and Type 2 breakouts. 

Do not be sceptic about breakout strategies. Just accept the market cycles.

These are similar in terms of reaching price target with a hard re-test.

At times of overall market volatility, we are likely to see more Type 3 than Type 1 (straight rally to price objective) breakouts. https://t.co/2aEEvVyiaP

$ASML met its price objective with a Type 3 breakout. Price can dip below the pattern boundary. This does not necessarily negate the pattern. Pattern negation level is the low of the right shoulder in this specific breakout. 

Breach of the low of last full day, makes it Type 3 as long as price target is met.
In volatile market conditions, we get more of these out of line movements. The stock wants to breakout but due to overall market volatility, first attempts fail to attract the buyers.
It is not about being right or wrong in a breakout setup. It is about the math behind it. Accepting failed attempts as part of doing business.

This brings China's official gold reserves to a record 2,331 tonnes, worth over 9% of their total FX reserves.

The country is also the 3rd-largest central bank buyer year-to-date, after Poland and Uzbekistan, with a total of +27 tonnes added.

China’s demand for gold is accelerating.

Prior to the 2020 pandemic, this reading never exceeded 20.0% during the 2017-2019 period.

Looking ahead, 36.0% of US consumers expect to be financially worse off over the next year, the 2nd-highest since October 2022.

This percentage is twice the average seen between 2015 and 2019.

China's rare earth export controls are driving prices sharply higher:

Yttrium, used in defense, aerospace, and chipmaking, has skyrocketed +14,000% since April 2025, to ~$1,100 per kilogram.

Terbium, used in permanent magnets for electric vehicles and wind turbines, has surged +350% over the same period, to ~$4,500 per kilogram.

Dysprosium, used to strengthen magnets in electric motors and defense systems, has risen +450%, to ~$1,450 per kilogram.

The surge has been fueled by China's export licensing requirements imposed on April 4th, 2025, covering 7 rare earth elements, including terbium, dysprosium, and yttrium, in retaliation for President Trump's tariff increases.

As a result, exports of yttrium, dysprosium, and terbium are down -50%, -60%, and -50% respectively since April 2025, compared to the 12 months before the controls.

China’s export controls are holding back some key rare earths.
